Discussion: Osteoﬂuorosis is a rare condition that results in
individuals exposed to high level of ﬂuoride in the air or food/
drink, and results in an array of bony abnormalities such as oste-
omalacia, osteosclerosis, and/or exostoses. When such bony irreg-
ularities occur at humeral heads and near bicepital grooves,
repetitive mechanical shears on supraspinatous tendons and
proximal long head of biceps tendons in the subacromial space can
lead one to the development of patient ’s shoulder tendinosis.
Conclusions: We present a unique case of atraumatic bilateral
supraspinatous and biceps tendinosis secondary to diffuse exostosis
of humerus attributed to osteo ﬂuorosis.
Poster 217
Presentation of Rhabdomyolysis in the Autoimmune
Variant of Stiff-Person Syndrome.
Xing Zhao, MD (University of Irvine Medical Center,
Orange, CA, United States); Hamilton Chen, MD; Die-
mha Hoang, MD; Audrey Huang, MD.
Disclosures: X. Zhao, No Disclosures: I Have Nothing To
Disclose.
Case Description: A 56-year-old man with past medical history
signiﬁcant for multiple spinal surgeries, chronic back pain, hyper-
tension, and hyperlipidemia who presented with fever, leukocytosis,
rhabdomyolysis, and progressively increasing muscle spasms. Patient
presented with creatine kinase level over 24,000, white blood cell
count of approximately 20,000, and elevated creatine of 1.65. Patient
reported that his back and lower extremity spasms started in 2010
after back surgery and described the episodes as a tightening of his
abdominal muscles followed by lower extremity jerking. Patient had
previously undergone extensive workup with brain MRI the year
before, with no visible abnormalies observed. Patient underwent
C-spine MRI which showed multi-level disk protrusion with no
spinal cord compromise. Patients had also undergone T-spine/L-spine
MRI which showed no spinal or foraminal compromise with multi-
level laminectomy and fusion. Blood and urine cultures were pan
negative for patient since admission. The anti-GAD antibody titer
ordered earlier to admission was found to be markedly elevated at
>250 (ref range 0-5), consistent with the autoimmune variant of Stiff-
Person Syndrome (SPS).
Setting: Tertiary Care Hospital.
Results or Clinical Course: Patient was subsequently treated
with IVIG. From his initial presentation with rhabdomyolysis, the
patient’s creatine kinase level and leukocytosis had trended down to
normal limits within two to three weeks.
Discussion: SPS has typically been divided into three different
categories. The autoimmune variant group describe patients with
anti-GAD, anti-islet-cell, as well as other autoantibodies. SPS
patients with the paraneoplastic variant does not feature the pres-
ence of anti-GAD, anti-islet cell antibodies. Rather, paraneoplastic
variants are often associated with the presence of anti-amphiphysin
antibodies. The third category of SPS is the idiopathic variant that
include patients without autoantibody production or other clini-
cally apparent disease processes. This is the ﬁrst reported case, to
our knowledge, of the occurrence of rhabdomyolysis in a patient
with the autoimmune variant of SPS.
Conclusions: Rhabdomyolysis is a possible presentation in
patients with the autoimmune variant of SPS.
Poster 218
Is This Shoulder Really Frozen? Sonographic
Measurement of Glenohumeral Joint Capsule

Thickness May Aid in the Diagnosis of Adhesive
Capsulitis: A Case Series.
Miranda B. Smith, MD (UMDNJ/NJMS, Newark, NJ,
United States); Todd P. Stitik, MD; Thomas B. Clark, DC,
RVT, RMSK.
Disclosures: M. B. Smith, No Disclosures: I Have Nothing To
Disclose.
Objective: To examine the potential utility of sonographic
measurement of glenohumeral capsular thickening as a diag-
nostic tool in patients presenting with symptoms of adhesive
capsulitis.
Design: Case Series.
Setting: Outpatient Physiatric Of ﬁce.
Participants: Four patients, ages ranging from 52-62 years, with
known unilateral adhesive capsulitis diagnosed clinically and/or by
glenohumeral arthrogram.
Interventions: Not applicable.
Main Outcome Measures: The glenohumeral joint capsule
was examined with patients seated next to an exam table with arm
forward ﬂexed to approximately 90 degrees and their hand resting
on the exam table. A high frequency linear probe was placed within
the axilla to obtain a longitudinal view of the humeral head and
glenoid with visualization of the inferior aspect of the glenohumeral
joint capsule. Capsular thickness of both the affected and unaf-
fected shoulders
was measured from the humeral neck to the
outermost part of the joint capsule.
Results or Clinical Course: Average glenohumeral capsular
thickness measured from the axilla was greater on the affected side
(0.65 cm) when compared with the non-affected side (0.36 cm)
(p¼.029).
Conclusions: The prompt diagnosis of adhesive capsulitis can
present signiﬁcant challenges to practitioners attempting to differ-
entiate it from other painful shoulder conditions. Magnetic reso-
nance arthrography demonstrating capsular thickening within the
axillary recess has shown promise as a diagnostic aid in several
recent studies, however direct sonographic measurement of
capsular thickness in patients with adhesive capsulitis has not been
investigated. The technique described in this case series is non-
invasive, relatively inexpensive, and allows for the arm to be out-
stretched, which may eliminate capsular redundancy that could
complicate magnetic resonance imaging techniques performed with
the arm adducted. The statistically signiﬁcantly increased gleno-
humeral capsular thickness observed in the affected shoulder
compared with the unaffected suggests that sonographic measure-
ment of capsular thickness may aid in the diagnosis of adhesive
capsulitis.
